  city cut at M1: the default framing percentile (§9.5) tightens from 95 % to 85 %, which enlarges every district on
  screen, and the check re-runs. (The old bar, ≥ min(12, number of districts), failed by construction where the cut is
  smaller than 12 — at 7 500 and 10 000 inhabitants, `docs/validation/bench/fixall_pipeline_r2_quarters.out` — and its
  "MFCG size 80 draws 17" was not the plain sweep's 12.)

### 9.5 Furniture, framing and tools

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r3); drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r3

* **Scale bar:** metres ↔ feet, major and minor ticks, old-style figures (`onum`); accurate to 0.5 % at every zoom (O6 c).
* **Compass (XB08):** a procedural 8-ray design with ink and paper halves, rerollable per town: its stream is keyed
  from the town root's entity key (§6.1, §14 `TOWN_ROOT` — the seed key alone) with the concern `style.compass` and that
  concern's salt, so a reroll is a logged `rerollLayer('style.compass')` event and a link or a copy of the document draws
  the same compass (NF-D12). Auto-placement: candidates are the four corners and the four edge midpoints, inset 24 px;
  score = the sum over the display-list marks the compass would cover at the view (labels × 3, protected features × 3,
  buildings × 1, ways × 1, water × 0.2, paper 0) plus 0.5 × (1 − distance from the view centre ÷ the half-diagonal); the
  lowest wins, ties broken in the order NE, NW, SE, SW, N, E, S, W; re-evaluated when the view settles. The covers are
  computed where the display list is — in the tile worker, by `ObstacleSource.coverage` for each candidate box — and
  reach the main thread through §8.9's furniture query (NR-4). Dragging places
  it and the wheel rotates it; both are view state (§11.3) and pin the compass. Its view key `compass` is `trueNorth`
  (default: the needle points at model north, whatever the view's rotation) or `free`; the map's own rotation is the
  `rotation` view key about the frame centre (§2.9, §7.1: MFCG's Rotate as a view rotation, never a model change).
* **Grid (XB15):** kind none | square | hex (pointy or flat) | mesh (triangular); cell size in metres or feet (default: a
  round ground distance ≈ one tenth of the view's short side on a 1-2-5 sequence; for VTT 1.5 m / 5 ft); colour role
  `grid`; fades out below its legibility zoom (cell < 12 px); **skip water** clips grid strokes out of water faces (on by
  default for overview grids, off for VTT grids).
* **Title:** in the emptiest corner (NG's rule: the corner whose box covers the least mark area, the sum of its
  `coverage` record from the same furniture query); movable.
* **Legend (J04):** a gazetteer panel — an embedded title, numbered districts (always in `legend` mode; in `labels` mode
  only for legend fallbacks), lettered landmarks, the scale bar and the emblem; border none | single | double rule;
  position any corner (default: the emptiest corner other than the title's) or free; metric or imperial; label modes
  `labels` (default), `legend` (districts numbered on the map, MFCG's Districts = Legend) and `hidden`; plus the symbol key
  generated from the registry (O12 d). Position, mode and border are view state.
* **Emblem (M06):** a furniture slot `Emblem = { source: 'none'|'import'|'generated'; svg?: string; png?: Uint8Array;
  generated?: EmblemSpec }`. Imports are sanitised (no scripts, no external references, ≤ 64 KB). The base ships a minimal
  generator of our own: `EmblemSpec` = a field tincture from the palette's roles, one of eight partitions or ordinaries
  (per pale, per fess, per bend, chevron, cross, saltire, chief, bordure) and zero or one geometric charge (roundel,
  lozenge, mullet), keyed from the town root's entity key with the concern `naming.emblem` and its salt (rerolled by
  `rerollLayer('naming.emblem')`; NF-D12); off by default; drawn in the legend or a corner. Chose a minimal own
  generator plus import over import only because the legend should be able to carry an emblem with one click (MFCG
  fetches one from a third-party service), at a fraction of a person-week; chose it over a full blazon engine because
  heraldic depth is not a map-parity item.
* **Annotation layer** (numbered markers and a separate legend sheet); **north arrow**.
* **Measure tool (L10, L08):** an `@plat/app` ruler — click points for a polyline length in metres and feet; area mode for a
  polygon's area in m², ha and acres; snapping to way centrelines, face edges and vertices through the display-list index
  (8 px radius) — `RoleIndex.snap` in the tile worker, reached by §8.9's snap query and answered within one frame, the
  unsnapped point being shown until the answer arrives (NR-4); exact in world centimetres; a measurement is view data and can be saved as an annotation.
* **Framing (A06):** the initial view and the default export frame are the circle centred on the settlement centre with
  radius max(the outer enceinte's radius, the 95th percentile of footprint distances from the centre) × 1.08, fitted to
  the viewport's short side (no letterbox: the long side shows more context). River tails and ribbon tips beyond the
  percentile are outside unless the user frames them; a user frame is view state. Furniture sizes are CSS px × a UI scale;
  device pixels are handled by the tiles.

### 9.6 Names

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r5); earlier revision fixall/integrate-r4; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r3; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r1, drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r1

Names come from the original grammar of §10.4, conditioned on the model (a docks district for its water, a gate ward for
its gate, a street for its destination or trade — R16), and are drawn from the entity's `naming` stream, keyed from its
entity key (§6.1), only for an entity with no predecessor, under a town-wide `rerollLayer(naming)`, under an ids-scoped
one that names it, or for an unedited name whose naming inputs changed — a grammar row it used, or the corpus a field of
the culture or ancestry row that chose it names — a (row, field) slice (§6.3 case (4), §7.6; VD4-5); a successor takes
its predecessor's name and naming record with its address (VD2-10, VD3-2). **Uniqueness (LC-17)** within its kind —
districts, quarters and water bodies per town; ways per district, and tier-1 ways town-wide: in a full generation names
are resolved in id order, and a later entity whose draw repeats an earlier name re-draws on its own `…/attempt=n` (≤ 8),
then takes a distinguishing suffix; in a scoped regeneration or an edit, entities outside the scope are fixed and only
entities inside it re-draw. An existing entity is never renamed by another entity's creation, and the locality oracle,
which compares against a replay of the same log, resolves collisions the same way. When carrying brings two equal names
into one scope, the entity whose address sorts later re-draws, and the rename is reported (§6.3). Feature-conditioned
names are evaluated when a name is drawn; a successor keeps its name even where its features changed (§6.3) — features
are not naming inputs. Names are rerollable (`rerollLayer(naming)`, town-wide or with `ids`, §7.1), editable (`setAttr`)
and persisted; the word lists are spell-checked in CI. **Test (B-EDIT):** a block reroll changes 0 names and 0
`LabelEntity` records outside its scope; placement changes outside the scope are counted and reported as view changes;
selecting a user corpus renames exactly the unedited names drawn from the field it replaces, and no other name — not the
district names drawn through the same row (§6.3; VD4-5).

## §10 Simulation and content layer (FTG parity, with restraint)

*In plain words.* Like FTG, every building has a purpose and people: the town starts from how many people live there
and what such a town needs (our own tables, not FTG's), places those needs onto plots by rules, and derives households
and people on demand. What is needed to draw and edit the map is in the base; hourly schedules, a calendar, factions'
meetings and events are an optional module over the same ids, so the one-click map never waits for a simulation.

### 10.1 Scope and depth (judgment J-9; IMPROVEMENTS J-S adopted; the content locality contract)

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r1); drafted by fixall/draft-pipeline-r1

**Base must-haves:** the sequential roster (S2), the per-plot context vector, the eager allocation (S7b, S10a) and the
per-district placement (S10b), households and people derived lazily from their keys, typed open spaces, rule-placed
landmarks and furniture, a gazetteer via `query`. **Base schema from M1, materialised by the module:** the relation store
(family units, relations, memberships, postings), sub-locations, factions with roles and goals, religions, the government's
offices (§2.7), and the economy and personality schema stubs of D-32 (§10.3). **Optional module `@plat/sim`** (delivered at
milestone M4b (§16), after the relation store's schema, which is in the base from M1; never gating milestone 1, never in
the one-click path): professions ↔ workplace matching, occupancy and schedules as a query, the calendar and clock
with external time sync, factions' and religions' meetings, events as templates, relations by the family-unit model.
Restraint: the map stays a clean plan; content lives in data, hover, the gazetteer and export; one click never asks a
questionnaire. The product proposal's D-7 widening (schedules and the calendar in the base module) is rejected as more than
J-S allows for the first release.

**The content locality contract (FTG-9).** Content is global and relational (a family spans households, an employee works
across the town, a faction has members everywhere), while regeneration is spatial. So: (1) the allocation is persisted,
and a scoped regeneration re-places only its own scope's allocation — global rebalancing of content is a separate, reported
action; (2) once the module has materialised the relation store, a scoped regeneration changes no relation outside the
scope: relations of people whose households were superseded are carried over by the household's address (§6.3) or
dropped and reported; (3) the locality oracle and O2 (c) cover content and relation hashes as well as geometry. *Judgment:* chose
a relation store whose schema is in the base and whose data the module materialises once and then persists, over relations
re-derived on every read, because a re-derivation after any scoped regeneration would reshuffle relations town-wide; the
one-click path still never pays for it.

### 10.2 Roster (data-driven, replaceable; sequential and prefix-stable; our values)

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r1); drafted by fixall/draft-pipeline-r1

```ts
interface RosterTables { classes: BuildingClassRow[] /* {id, use, perCapita:[lo,hi], perOther?: {class, ratio}, min, max, firstAtPopulation, requires: ('water'|'coast'|'route'|'farmland'|'ore'|'stone'|'timber'|'fish'|'clay')[],
    outside: boolean, liveIn: boolean, cluster?: string, noxious, lifestyleBand, shopProb, priority, footprintM2:[p10,p50,p90], floors:[…], heights, coverageByBand, siteplan, subLocations: SubLocationRow[], openingHours: OpeningRow[], tags} */;
  institutions: InstitutionRow[]; government: GovernmentRow[] /* offices and seat classes per government kind */; religions: ReligionRow[];
  households: HouseholdRow[] /* size distributions by class */; professions: ProfessionRow[]; farm: FarmTable /* §4.9 */; names: NamePack; provenance: Provenance }
```

**The sequential roster (FTG-14; FTG's documented *shape*, `ftg-docs-params.md` §3.3 via the proposals; none of its 209
types, 80 nodes, 299 professions or 323 items).** A **virtual population** advances on a fixed grid of Δ = 10 people up to
the rung's maximum. At each grid point the target count of every class is a monotone step function of the virtual
population — `perCapita` or `perOther` ratios converted to per-person ratios, core versus shop pools, lifestyle-banded pools
with rare outliers (weights ours), hard `min` / `max`, **size gates** (`firstAtPopulation`), **resource gates** read from
`SiteResources` (no farmland → no farms, shops instead) — and every class below its target receives its next building, in
class-priority then class-id order. Every draw is keyed by the building's ordinal (`roster/<class>/<ordinal>`: shop or core,
lifestyle outlier), so the n-th chandler is the same chandler at any population. The run records each building's
**appearance population**; the manifest for population P is every (class, ordinal) that appeared at or below P.
Consequently manifest(P₂) ⊇ manifest(P₁) whenever P₂ > P₁ (property test on 1 000 seeds), an epoch's delta demand is exactly
the suffix, a population fall selects the suffix in reverse order, negative deltas arise only from declared circumstance
events, and §7.8's population control is monotone by construction. **Mode (COV-FTG-B06):** `rosterMode: 'minimiseUnemployment'`
(default: at each grid point, when the unemployed share of the virtual population exceeds a table threshold, the workplace
class with the largest weighted job deficit receives one extra building) or `'matchRatios'` (the configured ratios only,
FTG's alternative). Both are grid-sequential, so both are prefix-stable.

Output: demand per class with area / frontage requirement classes, district affinities, cluster tags, live-in flags,
outside flags and wealth bands; the **character vector** (mercantile / ecclesiastic / military / agrarian / squalid …)
shifts the ratios. **Government (COV-FTG-B13):** the blueprint's `government` circumstance selects a `GovernmentRow` whose
offices force seats — a crown seat forces a royal castle or palace, a seigneurial lordship a lord's castle or keep, an
ecclesiastical lordship a bishop's palace beside the cathedral, a chartered commune a town hall and guild halls, a merchant
oligarchy a merchants' hall — plus a military share (guard posts per 1 000 inhabitants; barracks at CITY and above near the
castle or the gates); the castle toggle `auto` reads it. **Religion (COV-FTG-B14):** religions come from `ReligionRow`s with
worshipper shares (the character vector shifts them), a practice share and clergy per 1 000; temples per religion are
proportional to its practising worshippers; each religion has a faction (§2.7). Then S7b allocates the demand, S10b places
it, and a bounded **plan–fit–reconcile** loop (≤ 3 rounds, inside each district's allocation) trims the lowest-priority
classes where capacity is short and types surplus capacity as yards, greens or vacant plots; population is honoured within
tolerance and reported (O7 a, e).

### 10.3 People, households, relations, sub-locations, schedules

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r2); earlier revision fixall/draft-pipeline-r1

**Households and people.** A person is a pure function `derivePerson(seed, key, tableVersion)` of its key — `(household
address, member ordinal, birth epoch)`; the address is what survives a re-derivation of the household's plot (§6.3),
whereas the household's lineage changes on New random — and of the person tables current when its household was created
(`Household.tableVersion`); it yields name, age, status, role, ancestry, height and appearance. **Pinning is an explicit
edit, never a view (LC-16, FTG-10):** opening a person in the gazetteer writes nothing to the document, the hash or the undo
stack; which people a viewer has seen is per-user view state. A table edit applies to households created afterwards; the
existing people change only through a diffed "re-derive people" action (§7.5 pattern). An epoch ages everyone by its years
through the key's birth epoch; births and deaths are epoch events of the owner-staged evolution engine. When regeneration
supersedes a household, its pinned or edited people are fixed inputs re-homed by rule to the household that inherits its
address (§6.3), or reported as orphans; the edit-lifecycle row for people is in §7.4. Storage: aggregates plus explicitly
pinned people — kilobytes for a 50 000-person metropolis (FTG PERF-1 answered; R14) — until the module materialises the
relation store, after which relations and postings are persisted (≈ 12 bytes per relation in the binary block; ≈ 1.8 MB raw
for 50 000 people at ≈ 3 relations each, reported per 10 k population as the O7 module metric).

**People model (COV-FTG-C01, COV-FTG-C08).** `AncestryRow { id, lifeStages: {name, fromAge}[], maxAge, heightCmBand, nameGrammar,
appearanceTemplates }` and a partnering matrix (pair weights and the child's ancestry rule) are data; the realism base ships
one human ancestry, and further ancestries arrive only through setting packs (§10.4). `Person.status` ∈ worker, unemployed,
retired, student, dependent; a dependent has a `carer` whose schedule it follows; when a carer is removed the household (then
the family unit) supplies the next carer by rule and the change is reported — a dangling carer is a reference-integrity
violation (§5.3). **Appearance (COV-FTG-C02):** appearance text comes from the §10.4 engine: weighted option tables per
ancestry, line templates with substitution, conditional lines (by gender, age or a value predicate), fallback lines and
article agreement — our own templates.

**The module (`@plat/sim`).** *Relations (FTG-9, COV-FTG-C04):* the first run materialises the relation store by one global
pass on its own stream (`content/relations`) in person-key order — family units, partnerships, parent / child, siblings,
carer / caree, friends, rivals, business and religious ties, affairs — and persists it with lifecycle and reference
integrity (§10.1's locality contract). *Work (COV-FTG-B11):* professions ↔ workplaces by greedy matching with id tie-breaks,
persisted as `Posting` records; after an edit only the postings of changed workplaces and the unemployed pool are
re-matched, in person-key order; unfilled postings are tracked and reported. *Sub-locations and occupancy (FTG-11):*
`occupancy(dayType, hour)` resolves the whole population in person-key order in two passes — primary behaviours (home,
work, study, care, following carers) from profession templates, then occupancy criteria (leisure, guest workers,
temporary residence) filling `SubLocation` capacities with their relax options — cached per (day type, hour) and
invalidated by edits that touch the people or buildings involved; `whereIs(person, day, hour)` reads the cache; resource
*provides / uses* edges on roster rows are data the schedules may read. Budget: one hour for 50 000 people ≤ 50 ms in the
worker, with a cost-model test (§12). *Calendar:* a configurable calendar (hours / day, days / week, rest days, weekday
names); the time is the view key `time` — `view.set { time }` sets it and the module's command `sim.advance { hours }`
advances it over the bridge (§11.3) — and occupancy is recomputed for the new hour; neither changes the model. *Factions (COV-FTG-B12):* seats on plots, an influence field
over districts (used by the prosperity drivers and the grammar), named roles with member criteria (predicates over person
fields) and counts, goals with methods and progress, a secret flag; role headcounts are reconciled with the seat building's
working capacity (excess roles are filled by members housed elsewhere; the reconciliation is reported). Government offices
and religions are §10.2's. *Events (COV-FTG-C05):* `EventTemplate { id, preconditions (predicates over relations, factions,
buildings), weight, effects: EditEvent[] }` rank candidate events per building; starting one applies its effects as logged,
undoable edit events. Data dictionaries (ages, genders, ancestries) are append-only and id-referenced so renaming never
re-colours (FTG DAT-3 avoided).

**Economy, personality and stat-block schema stubs (D-32; COV-FTG-B10, COV-FTG-C03, COV-FTG-C11).** In the base registry
from M1, empty until `@plat/sim` materialises them; every table is our own:

```ts
interface ItemRow { id: string; category: string; unit: string; basePrice: number /* in the setting pack's coin unit */; providedBy?: string[] /* roster class ids */ }
interface ServiceRow { id: string; providedBy: string[]; basePrice: number }
interface Stock { building: Id; item: string; qty: number }
interface PriceTable { multiplier: number; overrides: Record<string, number> }   // global price edits are `editTable` events (§7.6)
interface PersonTraits { traits: string[]; motivation: string; mannerism: string; hobbies: string[]; education: string }   // derived from the person key
interface StatBlockPack { id: string; attributes: string[]; base: Record<string, [number, number]>; professionModifiers: Record<string, Record<string, number>> }   // a named game-system pack, off by default (D-3)
```

The relation store answers the family-tree query (`{ kind: 'relations'; person; up; down }`, §11.2, §14).

### 10.4 Names, descriptions and setting packs

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r5); earlier revision fixall/integrate-r4; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r3; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r2, drafted by fixall/draft-pipeline-r2

An original English-fantasy grammar (D-6) in a Tracery-class engine of our own (rules with modifiers, feature guards,
weighted decks, conditional lines, article agreement) plus syllable and Markov generators over corpora of our own
authoring; folk-contraction as an EVO event (FTG's erosion idea; "≤ 3 syllables" a parameter); naming draws from the
naming concerns only — each entity's `naming` stream keyed from its entity key (§6.1), the quarter tree's
`naming.quarter` and the town root's `naming.emblem` (§9.5) — and a name is drawn only in §6.3's four cases — an entity
without a predecessor, a town-wide or ids-scoped reroll, or an unedited name whose naming inputs changed — a successor
keeping its predecessor's name and naming record (VD2-10, VD3-2) — so names never move geometry, and uniqueness follows
§9.6 (an existing entity is never renamed; a new entity whose draw repeats a name re-draws on its own stream). The same
engine writes **descriptions** — a district's one-line summary of its mix and features, e.g. a waterfront quarter that
also holds workshops and a green (COV-FTG-E10), and each building's description (§2.6) — and people's appearance lines
(§10.3); descriptions are regenerated when their inputs change unless edited.

**Per-culture generators and user lists (COV-FTG-L06).** Every `AncestryRow` and culture row names its own grammar and
corpora, so personal and place names can differ by culture; a user-uploaded list (plain text, one entry per line)
becomes a `user` corpus: a syllable and a Markov model trained from it at load, stored in the document as pack data (the
`packs` block of §2.9) with author `user`, selectable wherever a corpus is; selecting it is an `adjust` of the recipe's
pack list that enters it in the pack list as `user:<content hash>` with `shipped: false` (§2.9, §7.6), so a town whose
history selects it never emits a link (§6.4; VD2-8, VD3-3). The pack holds the corpus and the keyed row operation that
sets the chosen corpus field of the culture or ancestry row the user chose to it instead of the corpus it replaces, so
the binding travels in the pack's content and hash (§7.6); selecting it therefore re-draws exactly the unedited names
drawn from that field — never the row's other names, listed for confirmation (§6.3 case (4)); each corpus field of a
culture or ancestry row is its own naming slice — the (row, field) pair, hashed with the named corpus's content hash
(§7.6; VD4-5) — and every draw records its naming slices in the name's naming record (§2.8). Deselecting it is a second
`adjust`; the corpus's content stays in the document while the first names it (§2.9's pack set; VD3-3).

**Setting packs — format and loading hook decided now (DEF-10).**

```ts
interface SettingPack { id: string; version: string; author: string; date: string; licence: string;
  provides: { grammars?: GrammarDef[]; corpora?: { id: string; kind: 'personal'|'place'|'word'; entries: string[] }[]; ancestries?: AncestryRow[];
    religions?: ReligionRow[]; appearance?: TemplateDef[];
    rosterPatch?: { table: RosterTableId /* classes, institutions, government, religions, households, professions, farm (§10.2) */; baseVersion: string; ops: RowOp[] /* §7.1 */ }[];
    tablePatch?: { table: TableId /* the naming, culture and ancestry tables */; baseVersion: string; ops: RowOp[] /* keyed row operations, orphaned exactly as a rosterPatch is (VD3-2) */ }[];
    styleHints?: Partial<StyleSheet> } }
```

A pack is data, never code: schema-validated (`zod`), every entry carrying its author and date (the clean-room rule of
§17), loaded as one layer of the override chain between the shipped defaults and the preset (§7.6), and recorded in the
recipe, or in the `adjust` that adds it, by id, version and content hash; the content of every pack of the document's
pack set that is not shipped with the output version is copied into the document's `packs` block and stays there while
any event of the log names it (§2.9, §7.6), so a replay never depends on what is installed, and a link is emitted only
when every pack of the pack set is shipped (§6.4; VD3-3). **A pack's roster patch is keyed row operations, never a
positional patch (LC-22, NF-D8):** per roster table, the `RowOp`s of §7.1 — rows addressed by their stable row key, each
`set` carrying the hash of the base row it was written against (`baseRowHash`) and the table version it targets
(`baseVersion`). When the document's pinned version of that table has changed or removed the row, the operation is an
**orphan**: kept in the pack layer, not applied, and reported with the old base row, the new row and the pack's value
side by side, exactly as a user override is (§7.6); an `insert` whose key already exists is an orphan too. So a newer
table version can never silently misapply a pack, and a pack edits the roster by the same row operations as a user. A
pack's **table patch** is the same kind of keyed row operations on the naming, culture and ancestry tables, orphaned
exactly as a roster patch is; a user corpus pack is `{ corpora: [the uploaded list], tablePatch: [one set on the chosen
culture or ancestry row's corpus field] }`, so the binding the user chose is part of the pack's content hash (§2.9,
§7.6; VD3-2). The base ships exactly one pack, our original English-fantasy set; further packs' contents are the owner's
adopted default "setting packs later" (D-6), and adding one is a file, not a code change.

## §11 Export and interop

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r1); drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r1

*In plain words.* One saved file holds everything (the recipe, the edits, the town); every other format — SVG with
layers, PNG at print size, GeoJSON for GIS tools, virtual-tabletop scenes with walls and doors, 3-D models — is a view
of that file. The generator runs without a screen (for tests and batch work) and can be embedded in another web page:
the page keeps the town in a background worker and receives finished pictures, so it never stalls. When several people
share one town — a game master and players — the host program keeps the one true copy and each generator only proposes
changes to it, so everyone always sees the same town. Nothing depends on a server of ours.

### 11.1 Formats

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r5); drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r5; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r4; drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r4; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r3, drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r3

| target | mapping | notes |
|---|---|---|
| **native `.plat`** | §2.9; round trip byte-identical | the canonical form; import of our own export (MFCG cannot re-import its export; FTG's export ≠ its edit format) |
| **JSON schema** | published, versioned (generated from the `zod` types); entities by id with containment | the API's response type |
| **compact twin** | CBOR with typed-array tags; varint zig-zag int32 cm in **world** coordinates, the settlement centre stored in the header, so it is an encoding of the same schema (FTG-21) | embeds and sharing; a decoder is part of the library |
| **GeoJSON** (RFC 7946) | two declared variants (N-14, below): the default **strict RFC 7946** file in WGS84 longitude / latitude through the geo anchor, and the **metric** file by prior arrangement; neither has a `crs` member. One FeatureCollection per layer; one feature per entity with `id` (its address, §6.3), `kind`, `layer`, `epoch` and public attributes; **districts included** (FTG omits them); ways as LineStrings with class and model width; faces as Polygons with holes, emitted without antennae (§3.6 (6)); MultiPolygons for face unions; walls, towers, gates and built bridges as typed features (a crossing `site` is not exported, §2.7); boundary treatments as LineStrings with `treatment` (VIS-8); **trees** per green entity as one MultiPoint of its instance positions (the §8.10 function at the finest band, overrides applied — integer-centimetre positions computed under §6.5's lint, so the file stays byte-identical on every host, NR4-3) with `species[]` (the §8.10 draw: the species kind of each instance), `crownM[]` and `leafType[]` in the same order, or one Feature per tree on request with `species`, `crownM` and `leafType`, or none (VN-158, XB32); model widths only, never symbol widths | the default file validated by an open RFC 7946 validator in CI and loaded by the scripted QGIS test (O11 d); the metric file checked for geometry validity and its sidecar against its schema |
| **SVG** | written from a transient display list the generation worker builds for the export (below; NR-5) at a declared band — the city band by default; the district band on request, after a size estimate is shown; the neighbourhood band only for a district-sized or smaller scope; `<g id="layer.ground"><g id="sem.building.footprint">` groups per layer and semantic; inside a group one compound `<path>` per (semantic, district), and a `<metadata>` JSON map from subpath index ranges to entity ids, so every entity stays addressable without an element each; trees as one compound path per green entity (crowns at the district band, the wood outline at the city band); text (N-13) by default as **outlines** — each glyph used is written once in `<defs>` as a path from the bundled face's own `glyf` outlines (quadratic segments as SVG `Q`), and each placed glyph is a `<use>` at the per-glyph position S13b computed, the label's text carried in an `aria-label` and a `<title>` so it stays searchable — or, with the option `text: 'embedded'`, as editable `<text>` (curved labels per glyph, straight labels as one `<text>` with explicit per-glyph x positions) in the bundled face embedded unmodified as an `@font-face` data URI (OFL permits embedding; no subsetting, §17.2); halos by paint-order in both; hatching as compound paths; symbol widths; the colour-matrix post operations as filters (§8.2) | budgets at METROPOLIS, city band: ≤ 650 B per building (MFCG measured 410–500 B per building: 0.42–0.66 MB for 837–1 512 buildings, 6.3 MB for 15 392) plus the text — outlines ≤ 64 B per placed glyph and ≤ 0.5 KB per distinct glyph, or each embedded face's base64 bytes once (≤ 0.5 MB per face, checked against the bundled files) — and ≤ 60 000 elements; CI opens the METROPOLIS file in Inkscape headless (export to PNG within 120 s) and checks every layer id (O11 h) (SCL-14, VIS-18); the outline file's Inkscape PNG and the embedded file's Chromium PNG each match PLAT's own PNG of the same frame within the visual-regression threshold (§13.4) |
| **PNG / tiles** | the band-streamed tile assembly of §8.8 at any DPI, rastered in the tile worker from the export's transient list (below; NR3-6); transparent background; per-layer transparent PNGs (the largest MFCG ask); print presets A4…A2 at 300 dpi | O12 (e): A2 at 300 dpi with no canvas larger than one tile band |
| **VTT** | Foundry-class scene JSON and **Universal VTT (`.dd2vtt`)** by the profile below, one scene set per model layer (underground / ground / sky) with its elevation | grid alignment error 0 px per cell (O11 g); no manual steps on import |
| **3-D** | glTF 2.0 binary (D-8): **ground as one planar partition** — the plat's leaf faces at the finest committed level, each boundary read once from the arena (§3.9) and each face exported once (no coplanar overlap), clipped to the terrain cells and draped (vertex z by bilinear terrain sample), material by role; **rivers as sloped surfaces** — the water level at each vertex is that of the nearest course station, falling monotonically downstream along S1's carved course; lakes, ponds and sea as level planes (GEO-40); buildings extruded from `baseCm` (FTG-13) to eave height with roof meshes to ridge height, per wing — each wing's `ring` (§2.6), its roof by the wing's kind as in §8.6 — each wing's foundation skirt extruded down to the terrain (§2.6); walls, towers and gatehouses as prisms on their bases; bridge and pier decks at `deckCm`; trees as instanced crown meshes (`EXT_mesh_gpu_instancing`, positions from §8.10), one instancing node per (green entity, crown class) whose `extras` carry the entity's address and, per instance in instance order, `species`, `crownM` and `leafType` (XB32). OBJ as a flat secondary (one mesh per entity, unlike MFCG's merged OBJ) | shadows, glTF and CityJSON agree by construction (heights are model data) |
| **CityJSON 2.0** | `transform { scale: [0.01, 0.01, 0.01], translate }` so every vertex is our integer centimetre (lossless); `Building` (LoD1.2 solid from base to eave; LoD2.2 roof surfaces), `WaterBody`, `Road` (lines with class and width, sampled from the way's width profile, §2.2 rule 5), `PlantCover` (greenery faces), `SolitaryVegetationObject` (trees from §8.10, one per instance: a `GeometryInstance` of the crown class's template, with the attributes `species`, `crownDiameter` and `height`; XB32), `LandUse`, `OtherConstruction` (walls, towers, gatehouses), `Bridge`, `TINRelief` (terrain); no `referenceSystem` (a local metric CRS); when the export has a geo anchor it is recorded in the root property `+platGeoAnchor { latDeg, lonDeg, bearingDeg }`, defined by PLAT's own CityJSON Extension and listed in the file's `extensions` member (below; DEF-5, NR-7) | validated against the CityJSON 2.0 schema in CI — the anchor-less file as it is, the anchored file with PLAT's extension schema given to the validator from the repository |
| **CSV / statistics** | the statistics record per generation with provenance (O6 d); people, buildings, plots | the corpus-calibration input |
| **permalinks** | §6.4's format; `&doc=` references resolve through the `DocResolver` of §11.5 | one line for unedited towns; refused, with the `.plat` file or `&doc=` offered, when the town needs a non-shipped setting pack, host content or a non-shipped style sheet (§6.4) |

**The two GeoJSON variants (N-14).** RFC 7946 fixes WGS84 longitude and latitude and removed the `crs` member, so the
default export writes exactly that. A **geo anchor** `{ latDeg, lonDeg, bearingDeg }` places the settlement centre and
turns model north by the bearing; it is an export option, remembered per document in the view key `exportAnchor`
(§11.3), and defaults to (0°, 0°, 0°) — the conventional "no real location" point, so a default export is never
mistaken for a real place. Each model vertex (x, y) in metres, rotated by the bearing, is taken as a transverse Mercator
easting and northing — scale 1 on the central meridian through the anchor, false origin at the anchor — and inverted
to WGS84 latitude and longitude with Krüger's published series to fourth order in the third flattening, evaluated with
`dmath` so the file is byte-identical on every host; coordinates are written with 7 decimals (≈ 1 cm), exterior rings
counter-clockwise and holes clockwise (RFC 7946 §3.1.6). Distances a GIS measures on the ellipsoid then match model
distances within a factor 1 + (d ÷ R)² ÷ 2 — at most 3.1 × 10⁻⁶, ≤ 5 cm, at the farthest corner of the largest frame
(≈ 15.7 km from the centre at aspect 2, §12.2). A foreign member
`plat` records the anchor, whether
it is the default, the document id and the output version. The **metric** variant — offered "by prior arrangement"
(RFC 7946 §4) for tools that want the model's own metres — writes x east and y north in metres from the settlement
centre with 2 decimals (the centimetre lattice exactly), no `crs` member, in `<name>.metric.geojson`, beside a sidecar
`<name>.metric.json` giving the origin, the unit, the axes, the document id and the anchor if one is set. Chose a strict
WGS84 default with a documented default anchor over the local metric CRS with a `crs` member because the latter cannot
pass an RFC 7946 validator and would be read by GIS tools as degrees, placing the town at meaningless coordinates; the
metric file keeps the lossless path for tools that agree to it.

**SVG text (N-13).** The export dialog offers `text: 'outlines'` (the default) or `'embedded'`. Outlines are read from
the same bundled face the labels were measured with (§9.2), so every consumer draws the glyphs S13b placed; the
embedded face travels unmodified inside the file (OFL-permitted; no subsetting, §17.2) for users who want editable text.
Chose outlines as the default over embedded text because only outlines draw the same glyphs in every consumer — an
embedded `@font-face` is honoured by browsers but not reliably by desktop editors (PLAUSIBLE; CI renders each variant
in the consumer it targets, §11.1's SVG row), and a substituted face at our per-glyph positions changes widths and can
collide — which is what "text identical on every output" (§8.9) requires.

**Where exports run (NR-5).** Every `export(h, fmt)` runs in the generation worker, which holds the document (§8.9).
*Model formats* — `.plat`, the JSON schema, the compact twin, GeoJSON, glTF / OBJ, CityJSON, CSV and permalinks —
read the model and §8.10's instance function (`Exporter.write(doc, null, opts)`). *SVG* needs a display list and label
placement at the export's own stop (§8.7), while the generation worker keeps only a 24-B index of the tile worker's
list (§8.1 item 6): the SVG exporter builds a **transient list** for the export's band and frame with
`DisplayListBuilder.build(model, band)` (≈ 4 µs per building at the city band: ≈ 21 ms at CITY, ≈ 54 ms at the
METROPOLIS target), runs S13b there at the export stop through `@plat/labels` with `@plat/render`'s `ObstacleSource`
and `RoleIndex` over that list — the code the tile worker runs, with the export frame as the visible region of §9.2's
scope, so the placement is the one the tile worker would compute at that stop and §13.3's placement digests test the
code both run — writes the
file, and releases the list. The whole is inside §12.7's ≤ 2 s, and the list is §12.8's export-time peak (≈ 1.9 KB per
building at the city band). A district-band SVG's list is counted in the size estimate shown before writing. *Raster
formats* — PNG, print and the `.dd2vtt` scene image — use a transient list too (NR3-6): the generation worker
builds it the same way, for the export's band and frame (including the live layers the export's layer set names, as
their providers stand at the request), and transfers it with the raster-export request (§8.9); the tile worker runs
S13b at the export stop over it with the export frame as the visible region — the first work of the export's class
in its queue, a resumable placement job stepped one decision at a time (§8.9, §9.2; NR4-2) —, rasters the export's
tiles from it by
§8.8's band-streamed assembly — each tile a resumable job in the queue's export class, below the view's work, and
each band's composition, read-back and encoding sliced the same way (§8.9) — streams the encoded bytes and a progress
message per band back, and releases the list; the generation worker wraps the VTT scene around the image. The export
therefore shows the model as it stood when it was requested, whatever is edited while its bands are rastered, and the
export dialog shows the bands done out of the bands total. Chose a transient list in the generation worker over
handing SVG to the tile worker because the SVG writer also reads the document (addresses, the supersedes table, layer
and entity metadata), which the tile worker never holds (N-4), and over keeping a second full list resident because
exports are occasional and the list is rebuilt in tens of milliseconds. Chose a transient list for raster exports as
well over rastering them from the view's list, because an A2 print takes up to ≈ 20 s and longer while the view
pre-empts it (§8.9), so an edit made meanwhile would reach the view's list between two bands and tear the picture —
bands above and below the edit drawn from two model states — and because the view's list holds the finer bands only
for the districts the view has visited, while the transient list is one model state, complete for the frame (NR3-6).

**The CityJSON extension (NR-7).** By the CityJSON 2.0 convention a root property outside the core schema is named
with a leading `+` and defined by an Extension listed in the file's `extensions` member; whether a validator rejects
an undeclared one was not executed here (PLAUSIBLE), so PLAT declares its one. `@plat/export` ships
`schemas/cityjson/plat.ext.json`, a CityJSON Extension (`type: "CityJSONExtension"`, name `Plat`, its own version,
`versionCityJSON: "2.0"`) whose `extraRootProperties` define `+platGeoAnchor` as an object of exactly three numbers —
`latDeg` in [−90, 90], `lonDeg` in [−180, 180) and `bearingDeg` in [0, 360) — and whose `extraAttributes`,
`extraCityObjects` and `extraSemanticSurfaces` are empty. A file with an anchor lists
`"extensions": { "Plat": { "url": …, "version": … } }`, the url being the address at which each release publishes
the schema beside the package; a file without an anchor — the default — has neither the property nor the member and
is plain CityJSON. CI validates both kinds with the extension schema supplied from the repository, so no check
fetches anything. A change to the property bumps the extension's version with the exporter's output version (§6.4).
**Measurement** at the CityJSON exporter's milestone (M3b, D-8): the anchored file passes the CityJSON validator with
the extension. **Pre-decided fallback:** the anchor moves to a sidecar `<name>.geoanchor.json` beside
`<name>.city.json` — the three numbers, the document id and the output version, checked against its own JSON schema
like the metric GeoJSON's sidecar — the CityJSON file carries neither the property nor the member, and the report says
so. Chose a declared extension over a sidecar as the primary because it keeps the anchor inside the one file a GIS
user moves around, and the sidecar as the fallback because it leaves the CityJSON file valid by construction.

**Identity in every export (LC-1, LC-28).** Every export carries entity addresses (§6.3) and the document's supersedes
table (tombstone → successor), so an outside tool that keyed data to an entity can follow it across re-derivations; ids
cross the API and bridge boundary as `<docId>/<id>`.

**The `.dd2vtt` profile (DEF-4).**
* **Scope:** a rectangle or a district chosen by the user — by default the current view snapped to whole grid squares.
  One scene image is ≤ 8 192 px on a side at the declared grid (default 100 px per 1.5 m square, so ≈ 123 m); a larger
  scope is split into a grid of scenes aligned to grid lines, or the user lowers the pixels per square (≥ 50) — the export
  dialog shows the choice before writing.
* **Fields:** `format` 0.3; `resolution { map_origin: {x: 0, y: 0}, map_size: {x, y} in squares, pixels_per_grid }`;
  `line_of_sight` — polylines in grid units from building footprint edges (minus door openings), enceinte faces, yard
  walls and hedges from boundary treatments (fences and railings do not block sight), and cliffs; `objects_line_of_sight`
  empty; `portals` — doors at building entrances (1.2 m openings) and gates (their opening), each
  `{ position, bounds: [two points], rotation, closed: true, freestanding: false }`; `lights` — the module's light sources
  in the scope, none otherwise, `{ position, range in squares, intensity: 1, color, shadows: true }`;
  `environment { baked_lighting: true, ambient_light }`; `image` — the scene PNG (base64) rendered by §8.8 at
  `pixels_per_grid` without the grid drawn in.
* **Per layer:** one file per model layer, its elevation in the file name and in a `plat` extension object; coordinates
  exact to the grid (O11 g).
* **Foundry scene JSON:** the same geometry as walls (`c: [x0, y0, x1, y1]` with movement and sight types; doors flagged),
  the same lights, a background image file, grid size and distance units, and journal entries from the gazetteer.

Chose to build CityJSON over leaving it deferred (D-8) because its integer-vertex-plus-transform encoding carries our
centimetre lattice losslessly, so the exporter is a thin view (≤ 1 person-week, M3b), and it gives GIS users a standard
3-D city path that GeoJSON cannot.

### 11.2 The embedding API and the worker boundary (SCL-6)

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r5); earlier revision fixall/integrate-r3; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r2, drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r2

```ts
type DocHandle = { readonly id: string };            // the document lives in the generation worker
interface PlatApi {
  generate(bp: Blueprint, opts?: { onProgress?: (p: Progress) => void }): Promise<DocHandle>;
  open(bytes: ArrayBuffer, opts?: { readOnly?: boolean; session?: string /* a host-assigned session (§11.3); otherwise the document's stored session, minted on first edit (§7.4; VD2-4) */ }): Promise<DocHandle>;             // .plat or CBOR twin; bytes transferred in
  edit(h: DocHandle, e: EditEvent | EditEvent[]): Promise<ApplyResult>;                    // an event may arrive with its `fates` filled (below)
  regenerate(h: DocHandle, scope: Scope, mode: 'keep'|'newRandom', opts?: { discardEdits?: boolean }): Promise<ApplyResult>;   // §7.1's Regenerate (keep settings) and New random
  adjust(h: DocHandle, param: string, value: unknown): Promise<ApplyResult>;                          // §7.1's Adjust, or Re-derive from Sk for a parameter consumed early
  confirm(h: DocHandle, token: string, fates: EditFate[], renames?: Rename[]): Promise<ApplyResult>;                     // completes an action that returned `confirm` (NF-D14)
  cancel(h: DocHandle, token: string): void;                                                         // drops it; nothing was committed
  undo(h: DocHandle, of?: number): Promise<ApplyResult>;   // appends an `undo` event for the handle's session (§7.4); `of` only for the `owner` role; a conflict lists the dependent events
  redo(h: DocHandle): Promise<ApplyResult>;                  // appends a `redo` event for the handle's session (§7.4)
  query(h: DocHandle, q: Query): Promise<QueryResult>;                                     // gazetteer, hit-test, whereIs, fates; ≤ 64 KB per page, paginated (kinds below)
  view(h: DocHandle, target: HTMLCanvasElement | OffscreenCanvas, opts?: ViewOpts): Promise<ViewHandle>;   // tiles flow from the tile worker
  setView(v: ViewHandle, patch: Partial<ViewState>): void;
  export(h: DocHandle, fmt: Format, opts?: ExportOpts): Promise<ArrayBuffer>;              // transferred out
  report(h: DocHandle): Promise<GenerationReport>;
  subscribe(h: DocHandle, handler: (e: ApiEvent) => void): Unsubscribe;
  close(h: DocHandle): void;
}
type ApplyResult =
  | { status: 'ok'; logHead: string /* §2.9 */; changed: number /* addresses whose records changed */ }
  | { status: 'conflict'; actions: ConflictAction[] }                // §7.1's dry run: the nearest valid position, the blocking lock, a stale base …
  | { status: 'confirm'; token: string; fates: EditFate[] /* the first 1 000; the rest by query 'fates' */; renames: Rename[] /* the case-(4) renames the dry run listed (§6.3, §7.3 item 4); the rest by query 'fates' */;
      counts: Record<EditFate['fate'], number>; scope: EditScope /* resolved */ };   // §7.3 item 4: nothing is committed until confirmed
type ConflictAction = { kind: 'moveTo'|'unlock'|'unassign'|'reroute'|'stale'|'invalid'; target?: Id; at?: PointCm; message: string };
type Query =
  | { kind: 'gazetteer'; text?: string; kinds?: string[]; page?: number }
  | { kind: 'people'; type?: string; race?: string; gender?: string; profession?: string; workplace?: Id; ageRange?: [number, number]; household?: Id; district?: Id; page?: number }   // COV-FTG-C13
  | { kind: 'hit'; view: ViewHandle; x: number; y: number } | { kind: 'whereIs'; person: Id; day: string; hour: number }
  | { kind: 'relations'; person: Id; up: number; down: number }   // the family-tree view (COV-FTG-C11), from the relation store
  | { kind: 'inView'; view: ViewHandle }                          // the "features in view" list (COV-FTG-A24; the non-visual route, J-S19)
  | { kind: 'fates'; token: string; page: number };               // the full fate list of a pending confirmation, then its renames (VD4-4)
// @plat/api/node — the same API over worker_threads, plus by-value helpers for scripts and tests
declare function generateDocument(bp: Blueprint): Document;
declare function exportDocument(doc: Document, fmt: Format, opts?: ExportOpts): Uint8Array;
```

**Confirming fates (NF-D14).** An action whose effective scope holds protected entities — Re-derive from Sk, Adjust of
an early parameter, a regeneration over locked, pinned, edited or assigned entities, "discard edits in scope" — or whose
dry run lists case-(4) renames (§6.3; VD4-4) — an `unlock`, `unassign`, `undo`, `redo` or `revert` that frees a name
among them (VD4-3) — runs its dry run (§7.1) and returns `confirm` with the fate of every protected entity (§7.3 item
4), every listed rename and a **token** = H128(the document's `logHead` ‖ the canonical bytes of the event without its
fates and renames). Nothing is committed. `confirm(h, token, fates, renames)` commits the event with those fates and
renames when the token is still current (the `logHead` has not moved) and the fates and the renames equal the dry run's
lists; if the state moved it re-runs the dry run and returns a fresh `confirm`, and a changed list is never committed
silently. Resubmitting the event through `edit` with its `fates` and `renames` filled is the same operation — the engine
commits when a fresh dry run computes the same fates and renames and otherwise returns `confirm` — which is how a host
bridge carries a confirmed action (§11.3). "Discard edits in scope" is a new request (`regenerate` with `discardEdits:
true`) with its own confirmation. `cancel` drops the token. Chose confirmation by token plus fate equality over a
fire-and-forget call with a "force" flag because §7.3 requires the user to see and confirm every fate other than *kept*,
and a replay that computes different fates must report a mismatch — so the committed event must carry exactly the fates
and renames the user saw.

| call | crosses | copy or transfer | bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| `generate` | in: the blueprint; out: the handle, progress events | copy | < 64 KB; < 1 KB per event |
| `open` | in: the document bytes | transfer | the document's size |
| `edit`, `regenerate`, `adjust`, `confirm`, `undo`, `redo` | in: events or a token with fates and renames; out: `ApplyResult` — `ok` (the new `logHead`, count of changed addresses), `conflict` (actions) or `confirm` (token, the first 1 000 fates, the renames, counts per fate, the resolved scope) | copy | < 64 KB per batch; longer fate lists by `query({ kind: 'fates' })` pages |
| `query` | out: one result page | copy | ≤ 64 KB |
| `view` | out: composed tile bitmaps and hit-test slices (§8.9) | transfer | ≤ 1 MB + 64 KB per tile |
| `export` | out: the file bytes | transfer | the format's size |
| `subscribe` | out: `ApiEvent`s (`doc.changed`, `view.changed`, report updates) | copy | < 64 KB |

The headless path runs the same worker code, and its model hash equals the browser's (text is not in the model, §9.1).
Ids cross this boundary as `<docId>/<id>` (§6.3). The derivation pool uses transferred copies, never
`SharedArrayBuffer` (§3.3), so no embedding host needs cross-origin isolation for generation; the tile worker's optional
shared columns (§8.9) remain the only use of shared memory. **Engine (§3.7, SCL-22):** the product bundle has no WebAssembly
dependency; if M0 triggers the kernel's pre-decided fallback (Clipper2-WASM as the single engine), WebAssembly becomes an
embed requirement and a host without it receives `E_ENGINE_UNAVAILABLE` from `generate` and `open`.

### 11.3 The host bridge — the host is the store (FTG-12)

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r5); earlier revision fixall/integrate-r4; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r3; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r2, drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r2

* **Transport.** `interface BridgeTransport { send(msg: BridgeMessage): void; onMessage(h: (msg: BridgeMessage) => void): void }`.
  Shipped: `WindowPostMessageTransport` (iframe hosts; a fixed target origin; incoming origins checked against the embed's
  allowlist) and `MessagePortTransport` (any relay — a browser-extension content script, a SharedWorker, a chat-bus
  relay; COV-FTG-N06). Envelope: `{ plat: 1, type, session, seq, logHead?, body }`.
* **Vocabulary (our own terms, FTG-22).** Host → PLAT: `doc.load { bytes | ref, role, session }`,
  `doc.apply { baseLogHead, events }`, `view.set { patch }`, `export.request { fmt, opts }`, `query { q }`. PLAT → host:
  `ready { outputVersions, schemaVersion }`, `doc.changed { baseLogHead, events }` (a local user's proposed events),
  `doc.applied { logHead }`, `doc.rejected { reason: 'stale'|'invalid'|'role'|'version', currentLogHead, conflicts? }`,
  `view.changed { patch }`, `entity.selected { id, kind }`, `export.ready { bytes }`, `query.result`.
* **logHead** = a 128-bit hash of (document id, edit-log length, hash of the last event), in hex (§2.9; our own term, FTG-22).
* **Convergence.** The host holds the canonical document and log. A client sends its user's edit as `doc.changed`
  against its `baseLogHead`; the host accepts only when that base is the current `logHead` — it appends the events,
  advances the `logHead` and fans `doc.apply` out to every client, the sender included — and otherwise answers
  `doc.rejected { stale }`; the client then applies the host's pending `doc.apply` messages, re-runs its own events
  through the dry run (§7.1) on the new state and sends them again, or shows its user the conflicts. An action that
  needs its fates confirmed (§7.3 item 4, §11.2) is sent only after the local user confirmed them, as an event carrying
  its `fates` and `renames`; if the state moved underneath it, the client's re-run returns a fresh confirmation for its
  user instead of resending, and every other client replays the event with those fates, reporting a mismatch if it
  computes different ones. Every client applies the same events in the host's order on the same output version, so every
  client's model hash is the same (§6.2) — after a load mismatch, once the owner has chosen (§2.9 step 4). **Test
  (M3a):** a host and three headless clients applying 1 000 interleaved random events — undo and redo from every client
  and one owner undo through a chain among them — converge to one model hash with 0 lost accepted events; and one forced
  load mismatch settled by an owner's keep while two editors edit on the replayed town: all four converge to one model
  hash, the editors' events re-applied on the saved town (VD3-4).
* **Version handshake.** On `doc.load` the client compares the document's **`outputVersion`** (§6.4) — not the generator
  version — with the output versions it can replay (announced in `ready`); when it cannot, it opens the snapshot
  read-only (its role drops to viewer, and it says so) as §2.9 step 2's frozen view does — checked by its chunks'
  content hashes only and labelled "made with o<k>; not verified by this version", never reported as a mismatch (VD4-1)
  — it never replays under another version silently.
* **View state.** Time, location, favourites, notes and public notes, view pins, layer choices, `stylePreset`, season,
  weather, frame, rotation, the compass, legend and emblem settings and the `exportAnchor` (§11.1) live in the
  document's view section outside the model hash (§2.9); each key is last-writer-wins by (Lamport counter, session id)
  and travels as `view.set` / `view.changed`. Time is the view key `time`: `view.set { time }` sets it and the
  module's `sim.advance { hours }` advances it (§10.3). `sim.advance { hours }` is a module-tier host → PLAT message: it
  advances the view key `time` by `hours` under the same last-writer-wins rule and lets the simulation module recompute
  occupancy for the new hour; it changes no model and logs no event (FTG-22).
* **Style is canonical; the preset a viewer looks through is not (N-15).** The document's style (§2.9 `style`: the sheet
  and version, its row operations, the ground-cover regions) changes only through logged `setStyle` events, which the
  bridge carries in `doc.changed` / `doc.apply` like any edit and which only the `owner` and `editor` roles may send. The
  view key `stylePreset` is a per-viewer choice of preset (for example a player looking at the `lit` family while the
  document is drawn in `ink`): it never writes `setStyle`; the chosen preset replaces the document's sheet for that
  viewer only, and the document's own rows (thematic overrides, ground-cover regions) apply on top where the preset has
  the roles they name, the rest being listed in that viewer's style dialog. Chose a separate preset key over treating
  the canonical style as a last-writer-wins view key because a viewer's look must neither rewrite the shared style nor
  silently diverge from it.
* **Roles.** `owner` | `editor` | `viewer`, given by `doc.load`. A viewer's client never emits `doc.changed` (model
  edits are disabled in the UI and dropped by the bridge) and emits only the view changes the host allows; the host
  enforces the roles as well. The host assigns one session per user and document and passes it on every load; a bridged
  client never mints a session or writes the `session` view key (§7.4; VD2-4). Load verification (§2.9 step 3) runs
  while the client's user edits; on a mismatch only an `owner` client may keep the saved town (a `rebase` sent like any
  event); every other client takes the replayed town for its own working state and reports the mismatch (NR-8). It keeps
  the `doc.load` bytes until the mismatch is settled; when the owner's `keptSnapshot` rebase arrives it installs the
  saved town from them and re-applies the events after `h₀` (§2.9 step 4; VD3-4); under §6.2 (iii) its comparison of its
  own root with the owner's `stateDigest` waits for its load's recomputation (VD4-2), a client still verifying stops,
  and a client that loads after the owner's choice takes the saved town as its base without asking — so every client
  converges on the owner's choice.
* **Logging (LC-31).** Every model change over the bridge is a `doc.apply` of `EditEvent`s, logged one to one; there is no
  bridge command that changes the model any other way. Undo and redo are `EditEvent`s (§7.4): they travel as
  `doc.changed` and `doc.apply` like any other event, the envelope's `session` is their `EditBase.session`, and a client
  never truncates a bridged log. A provider output refused at §2.9's cap returns the requesting edit as
  `doc.rejected { reason: 'invalid', conflicts }` (VD2-8).

### 11.4 Host inputs (DEF-11)

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r3); earlier revision fixall/integrate-r1, drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r1

A host may supply input only through these doors: (1) blueprint fields — seed, rung, population, intent, character,
circumstances, assignments — to `generate`; (2) edit events through the API or `doc.apply`, which are logged; (3) tables,
presets and styles as `editTable`, `editPreset` or `setStyle` events, whose content is copied into the document with
provenance `host` (source, date, version), so the document replays without the host; (4) a registered `ContentProvider`
(§14), accepted only after a **double-run check** (at registration it runs twice on the same input and stream; the two
outputs must be byte-identical, else it is refused), with every output it produces for a document recorded in the
document's `hostContent` block, keyed by (provider id, version, input hash), and read from there on replay; an output that would pass §2.9's 2 MB
cap on pack data and host content is refused at the call, nothing is recorded, and the requesting edit returns an
F-EDIT conflict naming the provider and the size (§5.2; VD2-8). So a
document never needs its host to replay, and host code — which the model packages' lint (§6.5) cannot reach — is made
deterministic by the check and the record. The mapping of SettlementForge's own data onto these doors is owner-staged
(after the standalone generators are mastered); this contract is its hook.

### 11.5 Sharing and multi-client use without a hosted service (DEF-12, COV-FTG-N07)

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r1); drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r1

* **Decision:** the product contains no hosted service. For multi-client use a host — a VTT module, a web page, or
  SettlementForge in its owner-staged phase — is the store (§11.3) and owns accounts and access.
* `interface DocResolver { resolve(ref: string): Promise<ArrayBuffer>; publish?(bytes: ArrayBuffer, access: 'private'|'link'|'public'): Promise<string> }`
  is configured by the embedding app. `&doc=<ref>` links are produced only when a resolver with `publish` is configured;
  otherwise the app offers the `.plat` file and, for a small edit log, the inline compressed log of §6.4. Access levels
  are the resolver's; the reference app ships a file resolver (local files and inline logs) and no network resolver.
* Chose host-as-store over our own sync service because the product is a standalone, backend-free library (D-4, D-21), a
  host already owns accounts and storage, and §11.3's protocol makes any host a correct store; reversing means writing a
  service that plays the host's role (low cost).
* Chose a transport-agnostic bridge plus the static VTT exports over building a Roll20 extension because an extension
  needs a Roll20 account and store publishing (outside a standalone program), and FTG's extension only relays the same
  messages that `MessagePortTransport` carries.

## §12 Performance budgets

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r5); drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r5; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r4; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r3; drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r3

*In plain words.* A town appears in under a quarter of a second, a city in under half a second up to about 25 000 people
and in under 0.6 s at 30 000, and a metropolis of up to about 48 000 people in about a second — the bar MFCG sets for
itself and FTG misses by several seconds. Because a bigger town has more buildings, each size gets a rule rather than a
single number: a fixed part plus a cost per building. Under that rule every town and every city appears within one
second, and so does a metropolis of up to about 48 000 people; the largest metropolises, up to 120 000 people, take up
to about 2.3 seconds. The same is true of building the town before it is drawn: the improvement plan's targets — a tenth
of a second for a town, three tenths for a city, one second for a metropolis — are met for 19 runs in 20 up to about
4 500, 17 700 and 59 000 people and for every single run up to about 3 400, 13 600 and 46 000, and the largest towns,
cities and metropolises take up to about 0.2, 0.5 and 1.9 seconds in 19 runs in 20; no single town may take more than a
quarter longer than its size's rule. Both misses are stated here for the owner to veto rather than hidden behind a
half-finished picture or a thinner town. Every step has its own budget, with the method that makes the budget possible
named beside it, measured on one named machine so the numbers can be checked. Compared with MFCG drawing the same number
of buildings, PLAT takes about twice as long for towns and cities and about five times as long for a metropolis, because
it builds what MFCG does not — real terrain and rivers, plots with yards, a plan for every plot, a roster of trades
placed by rule, greenery and non-colliding labels. That trade is stated here so the owner can veto it too.

### 12.1 Reference hardware and how budgets are measured (SCL-15)

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r4); drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r4; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r2, drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r2

* **Reference machine:** Apple M1 (4 performance + 4 efficiency cores) in a MacBook Air (MacBookAir10,1, fanless), 16 GB,
  macOS 14.7, Chrome stable and Node 24 — the machine on which every MFCG, FTG and NG bar in this document was recorded
  and on which the named mechanisms were timed (redteam-scale §7). The capture record
  (`captures/mfcg/2026-09-21T11-25-32/meta.json`) holds the CPU, 8 cores, arm64 and Node v24.12.0 but no memory size and
  no Chrome version (`chrome: null`); the model, memory and OS were read from the same host on 2026-09-25
  (`docs/validation/bench/fixall_rendering_r2_host.out`, N-27 b). Because the host is fanless, every timing batch starts
  after 30 s idle and runs ≤ 60 s, with `bench/calibrate` run before and after it; a batch whose two scores differ by
  more than 5 % is re-run.
* **Low-end device** (O12 b's ≥ 30 fps clause; the `low` hardware tier): Intel Core i3-10110U (2 cores, 4 threads, UHD
  Graphics 620), 8 GB, Chrome stable — or any machine whose calibration score is within ± 15 % of it.
* **Calibration benchmark** (`bench/calibrate`, fixed inputs): 5-octave fBm over 256² cells, a bucket-queue priority flood
  over 256², a 20 000-node Dijkstra, a 100 000-element typed-array sort, and, in browser runs, a Canvas2D raster of 32
  fixed tiles. Every score is stored with the host's CPU model and core counts, memory size, OS version, Node version
  and browser name and version (from the user-agent client hints), so a stored score always names its machine (N-27 b).
  CI divides every timing by (runner score ÷ reference score) before comparing it with a budget; the reference score is
  stored with the goldens.
* **Where each budget is measured (N-27 a):** model budgets in Node 24 (worker_threads for the pool) on every tier, and —
  in the nightly tier (§13.8) — again inside Chrome's worker on the same seeds and sizes; where the two figures differ
  by more than ± 15 %, the Chrome figure is the one checked against the budget (the product runs in browsers) and the
  difference is reported with both numbers. Frame, tile, first-map and label budgets are measured in Chrome
  (Playwright, GPU on). p50 and p95 are over B-CITY's seeds per rung and water setting.
* **Timing on shared runners (NR3-4).** A CI timing that gates a budget — the cost-model sweeps (§13.2), the first-map,
  settle and query runs (§12.5, §8.9), the export runs (§12.7), the pool comparison and the re-timing of a max-clause
  outlier (§12.3) — is taken in the **timing phase**: last in its tier, alone on the runner (no other suite, generation
  or browser running), in batches of ≤ 60 s with `bench/calibrate` before and after each, a batch whose two scores
  differ by more than 5 % re-run, and the pool size recorded with every timing. A timing taken while other suites share
  the runner — the nightly B-CITY set, which runs beside the invariant suite, B-FUZZ and B-EDIT (§13.8) — screens and
  never gates: a generation it flags is re-timed in the timing phase (§12.3). The phase costs ≤ 20 min of the nightly
  budget: the sweeps and the first-map runs are nine sizes × five seeds in Node and in Chrome (≈ 1–2 min of
  generating), while re-timing takes at most 20 generations × 3 runs per rung (≤ ≈ 3.5 min at the band tops). Chose one
  timing phase over a noise rule per check because runner contention inflates every gating timing the same way — a
  five-seed p95 is in effect a maximum — so every check that compares a time with a bound is protected once.
* **Confirming milestones.** Each budget of §12.3–§12.8 names the milestone that confirms it and the pre-decided change
  taken if it misses: model laws M1 (TOWN, CITY) and M2b (METROPOLIS), §12.3; first map, settle and re-raster M1 and
  M2b, §12.5; exports M1 (SVG, PNG) and M2b (METROPOLIS SVG), §12.7; memory M1 and M2b, and the load-verification case
  at M2a, §12.8.
* **Budgets never change output.** A missed budget is reported, never answered at run time by computing something
  coarser (F-BUDGET-TIME is reporting-only, GEO-2); the pre-decided changes are configuration decisions taken once at a
  milestone and reported, and none of them changes the model.

### 12.3 Model budgets on the one-click path

> PENDING FABLE REVIEW — revised by opus stand-in (fixall/integrate-r4); drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r4; earlier revision fixall/integrate-r3, drafted by fixall/draft-rendering-r3

The primary configuration is one generation worker plus a **derivation pool** of up to three workers for the
per-district stages (S10 plots, S10b placement, S11 site plans, per-district greenery) — and the hinterland unit, which
runs the same stages on the generation worker concurrently (§4.1) — which run after the eager S10a allocation (LC-2) as
pure functions of eager upstream state and their district's own sub-stream, merged in district lineage order (§4.1,
§6.3; never address order, which a carried district does not share with its lineage — NF-D13, NF-P12). The
single-worker column is the pre-decided fallback: on the low tier, in hosts that forbid extra workers, and at every size
where the pool measures slower than a single worker or fails the digest check (*Which configuration is primary*, below;
NR3-1).

| rung | model p50 / p95 (pool) | per building at p95 | MFCG at the matched size | ratio at p95 | single-worker fallback p95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TOWN | 76 / 100 ms | 75 µs | 57 ms (39 µs per building) | 1.8× | 115 ms |
| CITY | 255 / 300 ms | 58 µs | 131 ms (25 µs) | 2.3× | 400 ms |
| METROPOLIS | 609 / 800 ms | 59 µs | 156 ms (12 µs) | 5.1× | 1 000 ms |

**Per-rung cost laws** (p95; used for every size inside a band, and fitted by the cost-model tests, §13.2): with the
pool, TOWN ≤ 20 ms + 60 µs × buildings; CITY ≤ 40 ms + 50 µs × buildings; METROPOLIS ≤ 100 ms + 52 µs × buildings (at
the 35 000-building cap: ≤ 1.9 s). Single-worker, through the fallback column's p95 at the same building counts: TOWN
≤ 20 ms + 71 µs × buildings; CITY ≤ 40 ms + 69 µs; METROPOLIS ≤ 100 ms + 67 µs. The table's rows are these laws at
1 333, 5 200 and 13 460 buildings — so its per-building column is 100 ÷ 1 333 = 75 µs, 300 ÷ 5 200 = 58 µs and
800 ÷ 13 460 = 59 µs (NR3-5) — and its p50 column is §12.4's critical path, the pool's frozen copies with their static
index partitions included (VK3-6); §12.5 adds the first frame to them.

**Where O3 (d)'s bars hold, and the declared miss (NR-1).** `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md` O3 (d) asks for model time "p50 /
p95 / max per size class within budget" at TOWN ≤ 100 ms, CITY ≤ 300 ms and METROPOLIS ≤ 1 s. Size follows population
inside a rung (§1.1), so — as for the first map (§12.5, N-2) — the bars are read over every size a rung builds, never
at its target alone, and checked against the laws above. The **max clause**: no generation takes more than 1.25 × its
own law, T_i ≤ 1.25 × L(B_i) with B_i its building count. p50 has no law of its own; since p50 ≤ p95, the bar is claimed
for p50 wherever it holds for p95. Values (`docs/validation/bench/fixall_rendering_r3_budgets.out`):

| rung (O3 (d) bar) | p95 at the band bottom / the default request / the top | p95 bar holds up to | max bound at the top | max bar holds up to | single worker: p95 bar holds up to |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TOWN (100 ms) | 46 ms / 92–110 ms / 196 ms | B ≤ 1 333 (≈ 4 500 people) | 246 ms | B ≤ 1 000 (≈ 3 400 people) | B ≤ 1 127 (≈ 3 800 people) |
| CITY (300 ms) | 187 ms / 265–340 ms / 481 ms | B ≤ 5 200 (≈ 17 700 people) | 601 ms | B ≤ 4 000 (≈ 13 600 people) | B ≤ 3 768 (≈ 12 800 people) |
| METROPOLIS (1 s) | 559 ms / 724–880 ms / 1 920 ms | B ≤ 17 300 (≈ 58 800 people) | 2 400 ms | B ≤ 13 460 (≈ 45 800 people) | B ≤ 13 433 (≈ 45 700 people) |

The band ends are §12.5's (440 → 2 940, 2 940 → 8 820 and 8 820 → 35 000 buildings); "the default request" is each
rung's target population over §12.2's building range, so the default TOWN request itself lands at 92–110 ms and the
default CITY request at 265–340 ms — the first table's 100 and 300 ms are the laws at 1 333 and 5 200 buildings.

**Declared for the owner's veto:** chose to keep every plot, site plan and building on the one-click model path at every
size (J-R7, J-I2; the owner's plot-model ruling) over holding O3 (d)'s bars across each band, so the bars are met for
p95 up to the sizes in the table and missed above them — by up to 96 ms at the TOWN band top (196 ms), 181 ms at the
CITY top (481 ms) and 0.92 s at the METROPOLIS cap (1.92 s) — and met for the max up to the smaller sizes of the fifth
column. The reason is §12.5's: the model's cost is linear in buildings at 50–60 µs each, while holding the bars at the
band tops would need a p95 of ≤ 27 µs (TOWN), ≤ 30 µs (CITY) and ≤ 26 µs (METROPOLIS) per building — MFCG's own range
(§12.9) — which only taking plot and site-plan detail off the one-click path could reach. Reversal cost: high as a
mechanism (the plot model leaves the one-click path, against the owner's ruling); nil as a reading — reading O3 (d) at
the targets alone, as D-18 did before, reports "met" with the same numbers and hides the miss. D-18 and §15.2's O3 (d)
row carry the same declaration.

**Measurement and fallback.** The laws are confirmed by the cost-model sweeps (§13.2, §13.8: every band's bottom,
target and top, five seeds each), taken in §12.1's timing phase, at M1 for TOWN and CITY and at M2b for METROPOLIS —
pass: at every size, the p95 of T_i ÷ L(B_i) over the size's generations ≤ 1.10, each generation read against the law
at its own building count, since a size's building count varies with the seed. **Pre-decided fallback:** a miss
re-declares the law at the measured p95 as a D-18 amendment for the owner's veto (§12.5's path), and the tables here
and in §12.5 are re-derived from it.

**Which configuration is primary (NR3-1).** At the same milestones the timing phase runs every size of the sweep — the
band's bottom, target and top — with the pool (three workers) and with a single worker (pool size 0) on the same
generations (B-CITY-lite's 50 seeds × 4 water settings at that size, paired by seed and water setting), and the golden
run generates 200 seeds at pool sizes 0–3. The pool is primary at a size when (a) it passes the sweep rule above
against the pooled law, (b) its p95 there is below the single worker's p95 on the same generations, and (c) the model
digests are identical for pool sizes 0–3 on the 200 seeds. The outcomes are pre-decided:

* **(c) fails, or the single worker is faster at all three sizes of a rung** → the single-worker column becomes that
  rung's declared budget, the tables of this section are restated from the single-worker law, and O3 (d)'s clause is
  reported missed by the difference;
* **(b) fails at one or two sizes only** → each size range runs the configuration that was faster at the nearest
  measured size — the switch at the midpoint, in buildings, between two measured sizes whose winners differ — chosen at
  S0 from the request's population ÷ 3.4 persons per building (§12.2); pool size never changes the model (§3.3 step 5),
  so the choice is configuration, not output, and each range is budgeted by its configuration's law;
* **only (a) fails** → the pooled law is re-declared at the measured p95 as a D-18 amendment (the fallback above), and
  the pool stays primary wherever (b) holds.

A pool that runs exactly at its law passes (a): the default CITY request lands at 265–340 ms (the law at 4 500–6 000
buildings), where the single worker's law gives 351–454 ms, so the rule keeps the faster configuration. Chose to keep
the pool wherever it measures faster than a single worker, judged against its own law, over one bar at the target (the
pool's p95 ≤ 300 ms), because the law itself puts the default CITY request above 300 ms, so that bar would have
replaced the pool by the slower single worker exactly when the pool met its budget (NR3-1).

**The max clause, judged on confirmed outliers (NR-1, NR3-4).** The nightly B-CITY run (1 000 seeds × 4 water settings
per rung, §13.8) **screens** the clause: it records every generation's ratio T_i ÷ L(B_i) with its pool size. Those
timings are taken beside other suites, so each generation whose ratio exceeds 1.25 is **re-timed** three times in
§12.1's timing phase — alone on the runner, at its recorded pool size, with the calibration before and after — and is
a **confirmed outlier** when the median of its three re-timed ratios exceeds 1.25. When more than 20 generations of a
rung exceed 1.25, the 20 with the highest ratios are re-timed and the flagged count is reported: a regression slows
most generations, so the highest confirm it, while a contended runner flags a handful. Pass: no confirmed outlier. The
same rule judges the clause at its confirming milestones (M1 for TOWN and CITY, M2b for METROPOLIS). **Pre-decided
fallback:** a confirmed outlier re-declares the max clause at the largest confirmed median ratio (for example 1.4 × the
law) as a D-18 amendment, and this section's max columns are re-derived from it. Chose a max clause relative to each
generation's own law over one absolute maximum per rung because a generation's building count varies with its seed,
so only a ratio to its own law separates a slow generation from a large one. Chose confirmation by the median of three
solo re-timings over the maximum of the contended screen because one garbage-collection pause or scheduling stall of
≈ 60 ms on a ≈ 240-ms CITY generation — exactly the tail a maximum over 12 000 contended timings picks up — would
otherwise fail the gate with no change to the generator, and its fallback would then loosen the owner-facing promise
on noise; a generation that is really slow is slow three times out of three (NR3-4).
